meta.title: Who really said "when you are a Bear of Very Little Brain, and you Think of Things, you find sometimes that a Thing which seemed very Thingish inside you is quite different when it gets out into the open and has other people looking at it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, A. A. Milne wrote it — but not in Winnie-the-Pooh. It is the narrator's aside in The House at Pooh Corner (1928), chapter 6, the Poohsticks chapter.

answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and traceable to the page: the sentence appears verbatim in Chapter VI of The House at Pooh Corner ↗ (E. P. Dutton & Co., 1928) — the chapter that invents Poohsticks. Two things usually get lost in transit: it is from the 1928 sequel, not the 1926 Winnie-the-Pooh, and it is Milne’s narrator speaking, not Pooh.

source.heading: The passage in full

docMeta.dd: VI — “In Which Pooh Invents a New Game and Eeyore Joins In”
1928, E. P. Dutton & Co., Inc., New York
Milne’s narrator, as an aside about Pooh — not Pooh’s dialogue

source.excerpt:
“You didn’t really,” whispered Piglet to Pooh, so as to comfort him.

“I didn’t think I did,” said Pooh anxiously.

“It’s just Eeyore,” said Piglet. “I thought your Idea was a very good Idea.”

Pooh began to feel a little more comfortable, because when you are a Bear of Very Little Brain, and you Think of Things, you find sometimes that a Thing which seemed very Thingish inside you is quite different when it gets out into the open and has other people looking at it. And, anyhow, Eeyore was in the river, and now he wasn’t, so he hadn’t done any harm.
trail: The exact wording appears in Chapter VI of the complete text of The House at Pooh Corner ↗, digitised by Project Gutenberg from the 1928 E. P. Dutton & Co. edition — in the narrator’s voice, right after Piglet reassures Pooh about the stone-dropping Idea.
Wikiquote’s sourced A. A. Milne page ↗ independently places the line in The House at Pooh Corner (1928), Chapter Six — “In which Pooh invents a new game and Eeyore joins in.”
The 1926 Winnie-the-Pooh, the book most quote sites name, contains no instance of the word “Thingish” anywhere in its full text ↗ — a quick check that settles the book question.
Standard Ebooks ↗ distributes the book as free of copyright restrictions in the United States, and Project Gutenberg released its edition in February 2024.

author.name: A. A. Milne
author.heading: Who was A. A. Milne?
author.metaLine: 1882–1956 · English playwright, Punch humorist & creator of Winnie-the-Pooh
author.bio: Alan Alexander Milne (18 January 1882 – 31 January 1956) joined the staff of Punch in 1906 and became an assistant editor, writing humorous verse and whimsical essays; he served as a signals officer on the Somme in 1916 and later wrote for military intelligence. He was an established playwright and novelist — Mr. Pim Passes By, The Dover Road, the detective novel The Red House Mystery — before the four children’s books he wrote around his son Christopher Robin eclipsed all of it. Winnie-the-Pooh arrived in 1926 and The House at Pooh Corner in 1928; this sentence belongs to the second.

misattribution.heading: What travels wrong
misattribution.intro: The words are genuinely Milne’s — this is not a fabrication. What gets mangled is the book, the speaker, and the front half of the sentence.

items.why: Goodreads’ most-shared copy of the line is filed “— A.A. Milne, Winnie-the-Pooh” and it is listed on Goodreads’ Winnie-the-Pooh quotes page ↗. But the word “Thingish” does not occur anywhere in the complete 1926 text ↗. The line belongs to the 1928 sequel.

Round-ups such as Pan Macmillan’s Winnie-the-Pooh quotes post ↗ print the sentence under the bare label “Winnie-the-Pooh,” which reads as the character. In the book it is unquoted narration with no speech tag — Pooh never says it.

Milne’s sentence begins “Pooh began to feel a little more comfortable, because…”. Nearly every reproduction starts mid-sentence at “When you are a Bear…”, which quietly removes the reason the observation is being made — see the full passage in Chapter VI ↗.
Quotefancy ↗ reproduces the line with a bare “A. A. Milne” byline and no book title at all, which is how the book mix-up spreads unchecked.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Milne’s own narration in Chapter VI of The House at Pooh Corner ↗ (E. P. Dutton, 1928), describing Pooh’s relief after Piglet praises the Idea that got Eeyore out of the river.

context.heading: The chapter that gave us Poohsticks
lead: Chapter VI of The House at Pooh Corner is the one where Pooh drops a fir-cone into a river and accidentally invents Poohsticks. Later in the same chapter Eeyore turns up floating downstream — he has, he insists, been BOUNCED — and Pooh’s plan for rescuing him is to drop a large stone into the water to “hoosh” him to the bank. It works. Eeyore, dripping, declines to be grateful: “I dived. Pooh dropped a large stone on me, and so as not to be struck heavily on the chest, I dived and swam to the bank.”

Pooh deflates. Piglet whispers that he thought the Idea was a very good Idea — and it is at that exact moment, before the story moves on, that Milne’s narrator steps sideways to explain how Pooh feels. That aside is the sentence everyone quotes. It is a book about a toy bear making, in passing, an unusually precise observation about the gap between an idea in your head and the same idea out loud in front of other people.
context.detailsSummary: Why it is the narrator, not Pooh
detailsBody: In the 1928 text the sentence carries no quotation marks and no speech tag. The dialogue around it is punctuated normally — “It’s just Eeyore,” said Piglet — and then the paragraph shifts into Milne’s narrating voice: “Pooh began to feel a little more comfortable, because…”. Nothing in the passage puts the words in the bear’s mouth.

That distinction matters for anyone quoting it: attributing it to the character Winnie-the-Pooh describes a line that does not exist in the book. Attributing it to A. A. Milne, writing as the narrator of The House at Pooh Corner, describes the line that does.

sourcesVerified.claim: Chapter VI of The House at Pooh Corner (Project Gutenberg's text of the 1928 E. P. Dutton edition) contains, as unquoted narration, the sentence beginning 'Pooh began to feel a little more comfortable, because when you are a Bear of Very Little Brain...' and ending '...has other people looking at it.'
Project Gutenberg ebook #73011 is The House at Pooh Corner by A. A. Milne, original publication New York, NY: E. P. Dutton & Co., Inc., 1928, released 21 February 2024.

Wikiquote's sourced A. A. Milne page attributes this exact wording to The House at Pooh Corner (1928), Chapter Six, 'In which Pooh invents a new game and Eeyore joins in', and carries no Misattributed/Disputed section for it.
The complete text of Winnie-the-Pooh (1926) contains no occurrence of the word 'Thingish' — confirmed by a full-text search returning zero hits.
Goodreads displays this quote attributed '― A.A. Milne, Winnie-the-Pooh', i.e. to the 1926 book rather than The House at Pooh Corner.
Goodreads' page 'Winnie-the-Pooh Quotes by A.A. Milne' lists this quote under that work, attributed '― A.A. Milne, Winnie-the-Pooh'.
Pan Macmillan's Winnie-the-Pooh quotes blog post reproduces the quote under the bare label 'Winnie-the-Pooh', without naming The House at Pooh Corner.
Quotefancy reproduces the quote with only 'A. A. Milne' as attribution and gives no book title or publication information.

Standard Ebooks hosts The House at Pooh Corner and states the ebook 'is thought to be free of copyright restrictions in the United States', while cautioning it may be protected in other jurisdictions.

A. A. Milne (Alan Alexander Milne) was born 18 January 1882 and died 31 January 1956, was English, joined the staff of Punch in 1906 and became assistant editor, served as a signals officer on the Somme in 1916, wrote plays and The Red House Mystery (1922), published Winnie-the-Pooh in 1926 and The House at Pooh Corner in 1928, and had a son named Christopher Robin Milne.
The Internet Archive hosts a scanned copy of 'The house at Pooh Corner' by Milne, A. A. (Alan Alexander), 1882-1956.
